aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.prompt: Infant chest compressions should be performed with which technique?

options.a: Two fingers on the sternum just below the nipple line
options.b: The heel of 1 hand, or 2 thumbs encircling the chest
options.c: Two stacked hands, as for an adult victim
options.d: Two fingers pressing on the xiphoid process

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: The 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS guidelines dropped 2-finger compressions because they rarely reach adequate depth. Compress the lower sternum with the heel of 1 hand or the 2 thumb–encircling hands technique, about 1.5 inches (4 cm) or one-third of chest depth. If you cannot encircle the chest, use the heel of 1 hand. Skills testing now covers both allowed techniques.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-finger compressions were removed in the 2025 guidelines; they usually fail to reach 1.5 inches of depth.
distractorExplanations.c: Two stacked adult hands are too large and too deep for an infant chest and risk injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressing on the xiphoid risks liver injury; compress the lower half of the sternum just below the nipple line.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.prompt: When should the 2 thumb–encircling hands technique be used for infant compressions?

options.a: Only when two rescuers are present; a lone rescuer must use two fingers
options.b: Whenever the rescuer can encircle the chest; otherwise use the heel of 1 hand
options.c: Never — only the heel of 1 hand is permitted after 2025
options.d: Only during choking when the infant still has an effective cough

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: 2025 AHA BLS allows either the heel of 1 hand or 2 thumb–encircling hands for infant compressions. Use thumbs when you can encircle the chest; if you cannot, use the heel of 1 hand. Two-finger compressions are no longer recommended, even for a lone rescuer.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-finger technique is no longer taught; a lone rescuer uses the heel of 1 hand if they cannot encircle the chest.
distractorExplanations.c: Both heel-of-1-hand and 2 thumb–encircling hands are recommended; thumbs are not banned.
distractorExplanations.d: An infant with an effective cough is still a mild obstruction — observe and encourage coughing, do not start compressions.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.prompt: A responsive adult with severe choking (cannot speak or cough effectively) needs

options.a: Cycles of 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object expels or the person is unresponsive
options.b: Encouraging forceful coughing and waiting for the object to clear itself
options.c: A blind finger sweep to find the object, then abdominal thrusts only
options.d: Rescue breaths to push the object past the airway

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: 2025 AHA adult FBAO: for severe obstruction, give repeated cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive. Then start CPR and look in the mouth before breaths. Mild obstruction with an effective cough is still “encourage coughing.”

distractorExplanations.b: Effective coughing is only for mild obstruction; inability to speak or cough means severe FBAO and needs the 2025 back-blow then thrust cycles.
distractorExplanations.c: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; 2025 adult relief starts with back blows, not abdominal thrusts alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Rescue breaths are for an unresponsive victim during CPR; a responsive choking adult needs back blows and thrusts.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.prompt: If the first cycle of back blows and abdominal thrusts does not clear a responsive adult’s severe choking, you should

options.a: Switch to rescue breaths to force the object down
options.b: Stop the maneuvers and wait for EMS while the victim tries to cough
options.c: Continue alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
options.d: Do a blind finger sweep after each unsuccessful cycle

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Keep repeating 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the adult becomes unresponsive. Then lower them to a firm surface, start CPR, and look for a visible object before each breath.

distractorExplanations.a: Rescue breaths are for unresponsive victims during CPR; a responsive victim needs continued back blows and thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: A victim who cannot cough effectively still needs the FBAO cycles, not a pause while waiting for EMS.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind sweeps can lodge the object deeper; look for and remove only an object you can see.

options.a: 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts
options.b: 5 chest thrusts followed by 5 abdominal thrusts
options.c: 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts (heel of 1 hand)
options.d: 5 back blows followed by a blind finger sweep

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: For a responsive infant with severe FBAO, give repeated cycles of 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts (heel of 1 hand on the lower sternum) until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive. Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants.

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant liver; infants get back blows then chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants; start with 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of 1 hand.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only an object you can see.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts for a responsive pregnant or markedly obese adult. Children with severe FBAO now get 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts (2025), not chest thrusts. Infants get back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.

distractorExplanations.b: A child 1 year to puberty with severe choking gets 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts, like an adult — not chest thrusts.
distractorExplanations.c: A child with an effective cough has mild obstruction; encourage coughing rather than chest thrusts.
distractorExplanations.d: A responsive adult who can cough forcefully has mild obstruction; chest thrusts are for pregnant or obese severe FBAO.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Without an advanced airway, adult CPR is 30 compressions to 2 breaths for one or two rescuers. After an advanced airway is in place, compressions are continuous and breaths are 1 every 6 seconds (10/min). 15:2 is the two-rescuer pediatric ratio, not adult.

distractorExplanations.b: 15:2 is the two-rescuer infant/child ratio without an advanced airway, not the adult ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: A 5:1 ratio is an old pediatric teaching point; current adult CPR without an advanced airway is 30:2.
distractorExplanations.d: Compression-only CPR is for untrained or unwilling rescuers; trained BLS providers give 30:2 when they can deliver breaths.

distractorExplanations.a: The upper sternum is too high; compress on the lower half of the sternum in the center of the chest.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressing on the xiphoid can injure the liver; hands go on the lower half of the sternum above it.
distractorExplanations.c: Two-finger compressions are an obsolete infant method (dropped in 2025); adults use two hands, heel of one on the lower sternum.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Keep interruptions in compressions as short as possible — ideally under 10 seconds — so coronary perfusion pressure does not collapse. Rhythm checks and compressor switches happen about every 2 minutes, not as long pauses.

distractorExplanations.b: Pauses of 20–30 seconds wipe out coronary perfusion; compressions should resume within about 10 seconds.
distractorExplanations.c: BLS continues until ROSC, a valid DNR, or a trained team takes over — not a 10-second cap on the whole resuscitation.
distractorExplanations.d: The goal is continuous high-quality compressions with only brief pauses for shocks, analysis, or a compressor switch.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: Without an advanced airway, two-rescuer infant or child CPR uses 15:2 so the extra pair of hands can share breaths. A lone rescuer still uses 30:2 for a child or infant. After an advanced airway, compressions are continuous.

distractorExplanations.a: 30:2 is the single-rescuer pediatric ratio; two rescuers switch to 15:2.
distractorExplanations.c: A 5:1 ratio is outdated pediatric teaching; two-rescuer infant/child CPR is 15:2.
distractorExplanations.d: 50:5 is not an AHA ratio; two rescuers use 15 compressions to 2 breaths.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: Infant compression depth is about 1.5 inches (4 cm), or one-third of the chest’s anterior–posterior diameter, using heel of 1 hand or 2 thumbs. Adult depth (at least 2 inches / 5 cm) is too deep for an infant.
Infants and children use the same compression rate as adults: 100–120 per minute, with full recoil. Rate does not slow just because the patient is small.
Infant compressions land on the lower half of the sternum, just below the nipple line, so the heart is squeezed between sternum and spine. Avoid the xiphoid and the upper sternum.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Closed-loop communication: the sender gives an order, the receiver repeats it back, and the sender confirms. That read-back catches wrong drugs, doses, and missed tasks in a noisy code.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.prompt: Axial resolution is approximately equal to

options.a: One-half of the spatial pulse length
options.b: The number of cycles in the pulse times the period
options.c: Pulse duration times pulse repetition frequency

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Axial (longitudinal) resolution ≈ SPL/2. Shorter spatial pulse length — fewer cycles or shorter wavelength — improves the ability to separate two reflectors along the beam. Pulse duration × PRF is duty factor, not resolution.

distractorExplanations.b: Cycles times period is pulse duration (time), not a spatial resolution length.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse duration times PRF equals duty factor, the fraction of time the system is transmitting.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubling SPL would worsen axial resolution; the formula is SPL/2, not 2×SPL.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-physics-basics.explanation: Ultrasound is sound above 20 kHz, beyond human hearing. Diagnostic imaging typically uses 2–15 MHz; that MHz range is a subset of ultrasound, not the definition.
Acoustic impedance Z = density × propagation speed. Large Z mismatches (soft tissue–air, soft tissue–bone) reflect strongly; similar Z values transmit.

distractorExplanations.a: Frequency times wavelength equals speed (c = fλ), not acoustic impedance Z = ρc.
distractorExplanations.b: Density divided by speed is not a used ultrasound quantity; Z is density times speed.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency times density is not impedance; Z does not include frequency.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-physics-basics.explanation: Power and intensity both vary with amplitude squared. Doubling amplitude quadruples intensity, which is why output and bioeffect discussions track amplitude carefully.

distractorExplanations.a: The relation is amplitude squared, not linear in amplitude; doubling amplitude quadruples power.
distractorExplanations.c: Power is not independent of amplitude; it scales with amplitude squared.
distractorExplanations.d: Power is not inversely proportional to amplitude; higher amplitude means higher power.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-physics-basics.explanation: PRF is the number of pulses sent per second. Deeper imaging needs a longer listening time, so PRF must fall to avoid range ambiguity.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse duration is the time one pulse is on, not how many pulses are sent each second.
distractorExplanations.c: Duty factor is the on-time fraction (PD × PRF), not the pulse rate itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Period is the time of one cycle inside a pulse, not the number of pulses per second.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-physics-basics.explanation: Echoes from greater depth take longer to return. To wait for those echoes before the next pulse, PRF (and often frame rate) must decrease, or range-ambiguity artifact appears.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising PRF at greater depth invites range ambiguity because the next pulse is sent before late echoes arrive.
distractorExplanations.c: Wavelength is set by frequency and speed, not by imaging depth.
distractorExplanations.d: Increasing depth does not raise duty factor by itself; the system usually drops PRF instead.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Spatial pulse length = number of cycles × wavelength. Shorter SPL (damping, higher frequency) improves axial resolution. Cycles × period is pulse duration, a time, not a length.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Doppler shift fd = 2 v f0 cosθ / c. Shift rises with flow speed and operating frequency and falls as the beam–flow angle approaches 90°.

Continuous-wave Doppler has no pulse listening window, so it measures high velocities without aliasing, but it cannot select a depth (range ambiguity along the entire beam). Pulsed-wave Doppler has a sample volume and can alias.

distractorExplanations.a: CW cannot isolate depth; that range resolution is the PW advantage.
distractorExplanations.b: CW probes typically use two elements (one send, one receive); that is a construction fact, not the clinical advantage.
distractorExplanations.c: Angle still affects CW velocity estimates; cosine θ remains in the Doppler equation.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: From fd = 2 v f0 cosθ / c, Doppler shift increases when velocity or transmit frequency rises, or when the angle is closer to 0° (larger cosine). It falls at 90°.

distractorExplanations.b: A 90° angle makes cosθ ≈ 0, so the shift nearly disappears rather than increases.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher propagation speed in the denominator lowers the shift; it does not increase it.
distractorExplanations.d: A drop in operating frequency or a move toward 90° reduces the Doppler shift; the shift rises with speed and frequency at a given angle.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Acoustic enhancement (through-transmission) appears distal to a low-attenuating structure such as a cyst. The beam is stronger than the TGC expects, so the tissue behind looks brighter.
Mechanical index (MI) tracks cavitation risk. Thermal index (TI) tracks heating. Keep both as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), especially in obstetric imaging.

distractorExplanations.a: Thermal index tracks heating risk, not cavitation; mechanical index (MI) is the cavitation-related parameter.
distractorExplanations.c: Duty factor is the transmit on-time fraction; it feeds heating models more than cavitation risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Frame rate affects how often pulses are sent, a heating/duty-factor issue, not the primary cavitation index.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Edge (refraction) shadowing appears at the curved margins of a cyst or vessel where the beam bends and intensity drops, leaving a thin dark line distal to the edge.

distractorExplanations.b: As frequency rises the period gets shorter, so the two are inversely related, not directly proportional.
distractorExplanations.a: The sound source (transducer) sets both period and frequency; the medium sets propagation speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Speed divided by frequency gives wavelength (λ = c/f); period is simply the reciprocal of frequency.

options.a: Magnetic fields make the crystal change shape to emit sound
options.b: Electric current heats a crystal, which then emits sound
options.c: Certain materials convert pressure to electricity and vice versa
options.d: Materials convert electricity to pressure but not the reverse

distractorExplanations.b: Heating does not produce the ultrasound pulse; voltage deforms the crystal directly, and heat can destroy it above the Curie point.
distractorExplanations.a: Shape change driven by a magnetic field is magnetostriction, not the piezoelectric effect, which uses voltage.
distractorExplanations.d: The effect is reciprocal: the same element converts voltage to pressure on transmit and pressure to voltage on receive.

distractorExplanations.b: The beam diverges in the far zone, so lateral resolution degrades beyond the focus.
distractorExplanations.a: At the face the beam is as wide as the crystal, about twice its width at the focus.
distractorExplanations.d: The deepest region is in the diverging far field, where beam width and lateral resolution are worst.

distractorExplanations.b: The velocity must be squared; ΔP = 4v², so 4 m/s gives 64 mmHg, not 16 mmHg.
distractorExplanations.a: The factor 4 multiplies v², it does not divide it; ΔP = 4v² in mmHg with v in m/s.
distractorExplanations.d: The simplified constant is 4, not 8; there is no doubling for valves in the modified Bernoulli equation.

options.a: Peak velocity over time as a spectrum
options.b: Mean velocity and direction of flow
options.d: Tissue motion rather than blood flow

distractorExplanations.b: Mean velocity and direction are what color (velocity) Doppler maps; power Doppler shows signal strength.
distractorExplanations.a: A velocity-time spectrum is the spectral Doppler display, not power Doppler.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-velocity, high-amplitude tissue motion is displayed by tissue Doppler imaging, not power Doppler.

options.a: Areas where far-field TGC is set too high
options.b: Fluid-filled simple cysts and the bladder
options.d: Tissues with lower propagation speed than 1540

distractorExplanations.b: Low-attenuating fluid such as cysts and the bladder produces enhancement, the opposite of shadowing.
distractorExplanations.a: Excess far-field TGC makes deep tissue too bright; it does not create an acoustic shadow.
distractorExplanations.d: Speed differences cause range (depth) errors and refraction, not shadowing distal to a structure.

options.a: Mirror imaging across a strong reflector like the diaphragm
options.b: Refraction at the edges of curved structures
options.c: Reverberation from closely spaced strong reflectors
options.d: Propagation speed error from passing through fat

distractorExplanations.b: Refraction at curved edges produces edge shadows, not the tapering echo trail of a comet tail.
distractorExplanations.a: A duplicated structure across the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact, not comet tail.
distractorExplanations.d: Slower speed in fat causes range errors and displacement, not a dense trail of reverberation echoes.

options.b: Spatial pulse length times number of cycles

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplying speed by frequency gives the wrong units; wavelength is speed divided by frequency (λ = c/f).
distractorExplanations.c: That inverts the ratio; f/c equals 1/λ, so higher frequency would wrongly give a longer wavelength.
distractorExplanations.b: SPL equals cycles × wavelength, so wavelength is SPL divided by the number of cycles, not multiplied by it.

options.a: Shorten the pulse by absorbing the crystal's ringing
options.b: Raise the impedance above that of PZT
options.c: Focus the beam in the elevation plane
options.d: Improve transmission between PZT and tissue

distractorExplanations.a: Absorbing ringing to shorten the pulse is the job of the backing (damping) material behind the crystal.
distractorExplanations.c: Elevational focusing is done by the acoustic lens, not by the matching layer.
distractorExplanations.b: The matching layer impedance sits between PZT and skin; raising it above PZT would increase reflection.

options.a: Cosine is 1 so the Doppler shift is maximal
options.b: Velocity estimates are at their most accurate
options.c: Cosine is 0.5 so the shift is halved
options.d: Cosine is 0 so no Doppler shift is detected

distractorExplanations.a: Cos θ equals 1 at 0°, where the shift is maximal; at 90° cosine is 0.
distractorExplanations.c: Cos θ equals 0.5 at 60°; at 90° it is 0 and no shift is detected.
distractorExplanations.b: Angles near 90° give the largest velocity errors; keep the angle at or below 60° for velocity estimates.

options.a: A duplicate structure deep to a strong curved reflector
options.b: A structure displaced sideways at an oblique interface
options.c: Multiple equally spaced echoes at increasing depths
options.d: Dark bands distal to a highly attenuating structure

distractorExplanations.a: A duplicate image deep to a strong curved reflector such as the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: Dark bands distal to an attenuating structure are acoustic shadowing, not reverberation.
distractorExplanations.b: Sideways displacement at an oblique interface is a refraction artifact.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Laminar flow moves in parallel layers with a relatively narrow velocity range — fastest in the center of the vessel, slowest at the walls. Turbulent flow is chaotic with a wide velocity spectrum and often a bruit.

distractorExplanations.a: Plug flow is a blunt, nearly uniform profile at the entrance of a vessel; laminar (parabolic) flow has a range of layer speeds, fastest in the center.
distractorExplanations.c: In laminar (parabolic) flow the fastest layers are in the center and the slowest are at the walls — not the reverse.
distractorExplanations.d: Brief flow reversal can appear in triphasic arterial waveforms and still be laminar; reversal does not define laminar flow.
